metadata.name: pwd
metadata.description: Display the current working directory path

installation.note: pwd is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: pwd (print working directory) displays the absolute path of the current working directory. It's essential for knowing where you are in the filesystem, especially after navigating with cd or in scripts where you need to know the current location.
when_to_use: Verify where you are after using cd
Use in scripts to determine current path
See absolute path of your current location
Confirm you're in the right directory
Display current directory for documentation or logging

syntax.description: Display the absolute path of the current working directory. Without options, it shows the logical path (after following symlinks).

options.description: Print logical path (follow symlinks - default behavior)
options.use_case: Show the logical path as you navigated it (default)
Show the actual physical path after resolving all symbolic links

examples.title: Basic usage

output_explanation.format: Absolute path from root to current directory

elements.meaning: Full absolute path to current directory

output_explanation.notes: pwd always shows absolute paths starting from root (/). Use this to know exactly where you are.

examples.use_case: Quickly check your current location in the filesystem

examples.title: Physical path (resolve symlinks)
examples.description: Show physical path after resolving all symbolic links

breakdown.difference: If Documents is a symlink, -P shows where it actually points

output_explanation.notes: Use -P when you want the actual physical location, not the symlink path

examples.use_case: See the actual physical location when inside a symlinked directory

examples.title: Logical path (default)
examples.description: Show logical path (default behavior, following symlinks)

elements.meaning: Path as you navigated it, including symlinks

breakdown.behavior: Shows path including symlinks as you see them

output_explanation.notes: This is the default behavior - shows the path you see, even if it's a symlink

examples.use_case: See the logical path including symlinks (default behavior)

misconceptions.title: pwd shows relative paths
misconceptions.misconception: pwd might show a relative path based on where you started
misconceptions.reality: pwd always shows the absolute path starting from root (/). It never shows relative paths.
misconceptions.tip: pwd always returns absolute paths starting with /

misconceptions.title: pwd changes the directory
misconceptions.reality: pwd only displays your current location - it doesn't change directories. Use cd to change directories.
misconceptions.tip: pwd is read-only - it only shows where you are, not where you're going

misconceptions.title: pwd shows tilde for home directory
misconceptions.misconception: pwd might show ~ for home directory
misconceptions.reality: pwd always shows the full absolute path. Even if you're in your home directory, it shows /home/username, not ~
misconceptions.tip: pwd expands ~ and shows full paths, never shortcuts

common_pitfalls.description: Not understanding the difference between -L and -P options
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -L (logical, default) to see path as you navigated it. Use -P (physical) to see actual location after resolving symlinks.

common_pitfalls.description: Expecting pwd to show paths relative to a starting point
common_pitfalls.solution: pwd always shows absolute paths from root. Use relative paths in commands if needed (like ../parent).

related_commands.relationship: Changes directory; use pwd after cd to verify location
related_commands.description: Change directory, then use pwd to confirm you're in the right place

related_commands.relationship: Lists directory contents; shows what's in the directory shown by pwd
related_commands.description: List contents of the directory shown by pwd

related_commands.relationship: Extracts filename; use with pwd to get just the directory name
related_commands.description: Get just the directory name: basename $(pwd)

related_commands.relationship: Extracts directory path; use with pwd to get parent directory

best_practices: Use pwd after cd to verify you're in the expected directory
Use pwd in scripts to log current location or set variables
Use -P when you need the actual physical location (not symlink path)
Combine with basename to get just current directory name: basename $(pwd)
Check location before important operations in scripts
performance_tips: pwd is very fast - it's a simple built-in command
No performance difference between -L and -P options
Useful in scripts where you need to know current location quickly

additional_notes.always_absolute: pwd always returns absolute paths starting from root (/)
additional_notes.symlink_handling: Default behavior (-L) shows logical path including symlinks. Use -P for physical path after resolving symlinks.
additional_notes.scripting: Common in scripts: CURRENT_DIR=$(pwd) to save current location
additional_notes.prompt_integration: Shell prompts often include pwd functionality (\w in PS1 shows current directory)
